title: The five things we have seen in almost every learning-focused school.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Asked what five things a school needs to be learning-focused, Skelton lists those that schools can actually change, deliberately leaving out curriculum because most schools have little agency over it. His five are a shared definition of learning, evidence analysed and discussed in classrooms, consistency balanced with individual flair, involvement of every stakeholder including children and board members, and leadership that models what matters. He argues the common thread is building a tight, shared organisation around learning. The leadership section is the most detailed: leaders should spend real time in classrooms, hold colleagues accountable for agreed consistencies, and frame messages to parents around learning rather than activity. He grounds all this in what he and colleagues observed across many schools and invites readers to propose alternatives.
points: Schools need an explicit shared definition of learning, because collaboration exposes unspoken, conflicting meanings.
Learning-focused schools gather classroom-level evidence of learning rather than relying on exam results alone, and they analyse and discuss it.
Consistency across the school and individual inspiration must coexist, with agreed commitments that guard against haphazard repeated experiences.
Leaders earn their salary by modelling learning, sitting with students for extended periods, and communicating in terms of learning rather than activity.
quotes: Most classrooms and schools will never have everything in place, partly because schools and classrooms have too many variables and partly because that’s the nature of life. Only a very, very, few reach a level of almost perfection, even for a short time.
So curriculum is out of my list because schools don’t have that much agency to change it. I’ve chosen five things that schools, teachers, Board members and others can do something about.

If learning really is going to be the focus of every decision this community of people are going to have to make, there needs to be an agreement about what learning is, something that we can all consent to for now, even if we improve or change it in the future. That definition of learning, around which we are going to consent, has to be rigorous and defensible but also recognisable by and explicable to people who are not in the deep end of helping people learn.
Learning-focused schools don’t ‘hope’ that learning is happening in classrooms. They know. They know because they go there and look for learning.

There has to be discussion and conversation about the analysis with a view to actions that will either ameliorate problems around learning or build on strengths around learning. It’s these three things combined that make learning-focused school better; evidence about learning, especially from classrooms; analysis of the evidence; and discussion leading to action.

It’s a narrow line between the two. But the consent to be consistent and congruent with other colleagues is as important as the freedom to excite and inspire through my own individual interests and personality.

In learning-focused schools, leaders spend significant time in classrooms. Not two minute walk-throughs but time enough to sit with children and students to know whether learning is happening or not. They spend time talking with teachers about what they and the teachers have seen and how it might get better or might be celebrated.
